```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(TSP)

## Concorde is not part of the package. Chunks that need it are only evaluated
## if the executables can be found.
concorde_path_found <- tryCatch(concorde_path(), error = function(e) NULL)
has_concorde <- !is.null(concorde_path_found) &&
  file.exists(file.path(concorde_path_found, "concorde"))
has_linkern <- !is.null(concorde_path_found) &&
  file.exists(file.path(concorde_path_found, "linkern"))

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 5
)
```

This vignette shows how to use the Concorde TSP solver [@Applegate2006] in the 
R package **TSP** [@Hahsler+Hornik2007]. 
The Concorde TSP solver is one of the most advanced and fastest
exact solvers for the symmetric traveling salesperson problem. It uses the
branch-and-cut method [@Padberg1990] and has been used to solve instances with
tens of thousands of cities. The Concorde distribution also contains `linkern`,
an implementation of the Chained Lin-Kernighan heuristic [@Applegate2003] that
finds very good tours for large instances in a short time.

**TSP** provides interfaces to both programs via `solve_TSP()` with
`method = "concorde"` and `method = "linkern"`. The programs are **not**
included in the package and have to be installed separately. This vignette
shows how to install and use them.

```{r status, echo=FALSE, results="asis", eval=TRUE}
if (!has_concorde)
  cat("> **Note:** Concorde was not found when this vignette was built. The ",
      "code that needs Concorde is shown, but its output is not.\n")
```

## Installing Concorde

Concorde is free for academic research use, but is distributed under a
license that does not allow commercial use. Because of this license and since it
needs to be compiled for each platform, it is not bundled with **TSP**.

1. Download Concorde from the
   [Concorde download page](https://www.math.uwaterloo.ca/tsp/concorde/downloads/downloads.htm).
   You can either download precompiled executables for your operating system
   (if available) or the source code and compile it. Compiling Concorde
   additionally requires an LP solver (e.g., QSopt, which is also available from
   the download page, or CPLEX) and may need some adaptation on recent compilers.
2. Make sure the executables `concorde` and `linkern` (the latter is built
   by default in the Concorde `LINKERN` directory) are executable.
3. Tell **TSP** where to find them. Either put the directory with the
   executables into the `PATH` environment variable (before starting R, or
   using `Sys.setenv()`), or set the path in R:

```{r set-path, eval=FALSE}
library(TSP)

## directory containing the executables
concorde_path("~/concorde/")
```

`concorde_path()` without an argument returns the path that is currently
used and gives an error if no executables can be found. This can be used to
check the installation:

```{r check-path, eval=FALSE}
concorde_path()
```

To make the path permanent, add the call to `concorde_path()` (or the
`PATH` setting) to your `.Rprofile`.

## Solving a TSP with Concorde

Concorde works with any `TSP`, and with `ETSP` objects. We use the
`USCA50` data set with distances between 50 cities and compare the exact result
to the heuristics.

```{r concorde-solve, eval=has_concorde}
data("USCA50")

tour <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "concorde", verbose = FALSE)
tour
```

The tour is a permutation of the cities. These are the first cities in the
order they are visited:

```{r tour-labels, eval=has_concorde}
head(labels(tour))
```

Since the cities have GPS coordinates in the data set `USCA312_GPS`, we can
draw the tour on a map. The map is only drawn if the suggested package
**maps** is installed.

```{r tour-map, eval=has_concorde, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
data("USCA312_GPS")
coords <- USCA312_GPS[match(labels(USCA50), USCA312_GPS$name), c("long", "lat")]

plot(coords, cex = .5, col = "red", xlab = "longitude", ylab = "latitude",
     main = paste("Optimal tour, length:", tour_length(tour)))
if (requireNamespace("maps", quietly = TRUE))
  maps::map("world", col = "gray", add = TRUE)

## close the cycle by returning to the first city
order <- c(as.integer(tour), as.integer(tour)[1])
lines(coords[order, ])
```

The `TOUR` is an ordinary object, so we can compare it with a heuristic tour,
here the default heuristic (arbitrary insertion followed by 2-opt).

```{r compare, eval=has_concorde}
tour_heuristic <- solve_TSP(USCA50, seed = 1234)
c(heuristic = tour_length(tour_heuristic), concorde = tour_length(tour))
```

For `USCA50`, the optimal tour length is 14497. Since Concorde finds the optimal
tour, no heuristic can be shorter.

### Chained Lin-Kernighan

`"linkern"` is used the same way. It does not guarantee an optimal solution, but
is much faster for large problems. The number of kicks (random restarts of the
local search) can be set with the command line option `-R`. More kicks lead to
better tours but take longer.

```{r linkern, eval=has_linkern}
tour_lk <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "linkern", control = list(clo = "-R 1000", verbose = FALSE))
tour_lk
```

### Euclidean problems

For Euclidean problems, Concorde can work with the coordinates directly, which
does not require creating a distance matrix. This makes large instances
possible. We show here a small problem.

```{r etsp, eval=has_concorde}
set.seed(1000)
x <- data.frame(x = runif(100), y = runif(100))
etsp <- ETSP(x)

tour_etsp <- solve_TSP(etsp, method = "concorde", verbose = FALSE)
tour_etsp
plot(etsp, tour_etsp)
```

## Control parameters

Besides the general arguments, the following parameters can be passed on to
Concorde and linkern using `control` or directly as arguments to `solve_TSP()`:

- `clo`: a string with additional command line options. `concorde_help()` and
  `linkern_help()` print all available options. The options `-x`, `-o`,
  `-N` and `-Q` are used by the interface and cannot be set.
- `precision`: the number of decimal places that are kept when distances are
  converted to integers (default: 6).
- `verbose`: if `FALSE`, the output of the program is suppressed.
- `keep_files`: keep the temporary directory with the input and result files
  (for debugging).
- `seed`: passed on to the programs (option `-s`) to make randomized parts,
  mainly of linkern, reproducible. It must be a whole number between 0 and
  `.Machine$integer.max` (2147483647). If no seed is given, one is drawn from
  R's random number generator, so calling `set.seed()` before `solve_TSP()`
  also makes Concorde and linkern reproducible (this advances R's global random
  number stream by one draw). Specifying `seed` calls `set.seed()` and thus
  replaces the global random-number state. Do not also give `-s` in `clo`.
- `rep` and `two_opt` are not available for these methods.

```{r clo, eval=has_concorde}
## use fast cuts only (-V); this may not give the optimal tour
solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "concorde", clo = "-V", verbose = FALSE)
```

### Integer distances and precision

Concorde and linkern can only work with integer distances. The interface
therefore multiplies the distances by $10^{precision}$, rounds them and writes
them to a file in TSPLIB format (see `?write_TSPLIB`). A warning is shown if the
distances are so large that rounding errors worse than `precision` cannot be
avoided. Negative distances (for example, resulting from the reformulation of
an ATSP) are shifted so the smallest distance is zero, which does not change the
optimal tour. If you need to reduce the rounding error, scale your distances
or increase `precision`.

Infinite distances are replaced by a large finite value (see `?solve_TSP`).

## Asymmetric problems

Concorde cannot solve asymmetric TSPs directly. `solve_TSP()` reformulates
an `ATSP` as a symmetric TSP with twice the number of cities
(`reformulate_ATSP_as_TSP()`), solves it, and removes the dummy cities from the
resulting tour. This is done automatically with a warning that can be suppressed
by `as_TSP = TRUE`.

```{r atsp, eval=has_concorde}
set.seed(1234)
cost <- matrix(runif(100, 1, 10), nrow = 10)
diag(cost) <- 0
atsp <- ATSP(cost)

tour_atsp <- solve_TSP(atsp, method = "concorde", as_TSP = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
tour_atsp
```

## Shortest Hamiltonian paths

Concorde can also be used to solve related problems by transforming them into a
TSP. For example, to find the shortest path (not cycle) through all cities,
insert a dummy city which has a distance of zero to all other cities and cut the
tour at the dummy city.

```{r path, eval=has_concorde}
tsp <- insert_dummy(USCA50, label = "cut")
tour <- solve_TSP(tsp, method = "concorde", verbose = FALSE)
path <- cut_tour(tour, "cut")
head(labels(path))
```

The length of the path is the length of the tour since the dummy city does not
add any distance:

```{r path-length, eval=has_concorde}
tour_length(tour)
```

## Interrupting and troubleshooting

- If Concorde takes too long, interrupt `solve_TSP()` with `Esc` or `Ctrl-C`.
  On most systems, this also stops the Concorde process. If it keeps running,
  terminate the process `concorde` using your operating system.
- The error "Can not find executables for concorde or linkern" means that
  **TSP** cannot find the programs. Check the path with `concorde_path()`.
- If the executables are found but do not run (e.g., "exited with status"),
  run `concorde_help()` and check that the programs are compiled for your
  platform, are executable, and (on Linux/macOS) are not blocked by the
  system's security settings.
- Use `verbose = TRUE` (default) and `keep_files = TRUE` to see Concorde's
  output and inspect the files that were passed to it.
- Running very large exact problems can take days (the 24,978 city tour through
  Sweden needed almost 100 CPU years). For large instances, use `"linkern"`.

See also `?Concorde` and `?solve_TSP`.
